title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams currently using Jira and considering switching to Plane, possibly due to the core use case of issue tracking and project management, and the key reason being the desire for more control over their data and costs. Teams looking for a self-hosted solution with more flexibility may find this comparison particularly useful.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira charges per user, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, whereas Jira offers a more straightforward setup process.
* Scalability: Jira is designed to handle large teams and enterprises, while Plane is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams.
* Integration difference: Jira has native integration with other Atlassian tools like Confluence and Bitbucket, whereas Plane has a more limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Robust feature set for project management
* Large community and extensive documentation
* Native integration with other Atlassian tools
* Scalable for large teams and enterprises
* User-friendly interface
* Limited customization options for self-hosting
**Plane:**
* Free and self-hosted, reducing costs
* Full data ownership and control
* Customizable and flexible
* Suitable for smaller teams and projects
* Limited integrations and native features
* Requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance

## When to Choose Each
Jira is the better choice for large teams and enterprises that require a robust feature set, native integration with other Atlassian tools, and a scalable solution. It is also suitable for teams that prioritize a user-friendly interface and are willing to pay for the convenience. On the other hand, Plane is the better choice for smaller teams and projects that require more control over their data, customization options, and a self-hosted solution. It is also suitable for teams with technical expertise and a limited budget.

## Migration Path
1. Export Jira data in JSON format using the Jira API or a third-party tool.
2. Prepare the Plane instance by setting up the necessary projects, users, and permissions.
3. Use a migration tool or script to import the Jira data into Plane.
4. Verify the data integrity and completeness after migration.
5. Configure any necessary integrations and workflows in Plane.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users due to its limited feature set and lack of native integrations. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is the requirement for technical expertise to set up and maintain Plane. However, for teams that prioritize data ownership, customization, and cost-effectiveness, Plane is a viable alternative to Jira, and we recommend considering it for smaller teams and projects.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) with basic project management needs
* Teams with limited budgets and requiring a self-hosted solution
* Projects that require full data ownership and control
* Teams with technical expertise and a desire for customization options
* Startups or early-stage companies with evolving project management needs

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted, reducing costs for teams.
### Can I integrate Plane with other tools?
Plane has a limited set of integrations, but it can be customized to integrate with other tools using APIs or scripts.
### How difficult is it to set up Plane?
Plane requires technical expertise to set up and maintain, which can be a challenge for non-technical teams.
### Can I migrate my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can migrate your Jira data to Plane using the Jira API or a third-party tool.
### Is Plane suitable for large teams and enterprises?
No, Plane is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams and projects.
meta_description: Plane, a free self-hosted project management tool, offers more control over data and costs. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*

title: Zoom vs Jitsi Meet
comparison_markdown:
# Zoom vs Jitsi Meet (2026)

## Overview
Zoom and Jitsi Meet are video conferencing tools that enable teams to collaborate remotely. This comparison is beneficial for teams looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted solution, with a key reason being data ownership and control. The core use case for both tools is virtual meetings, and teams may consider switching due to cost, scalability, or specific feature requirements.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Zoom offers a free plan with limitations, while Jitsi Meet is completely free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: Jitsi Meet allows for self-hosting, giving teams full control over their data, whereas Zoom stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup Complexity: Jitsi Meet requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting, compared to Zoom's user-friendly interface.
* Scalability: Zoom is designed for large-scale deployments, while Jitsi Meet can also handle large meetings but may require more configuration.
* Feature Difference: Zoom offers a more comprehensive set of features, including virtual whiteboards and polls, whereas Jitsi Meet focuses on core video conferencing functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Zoom | Jitsi Meet |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $13.33+/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $666.50/month (50 x $13.33) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2,666/month (200 x $13.33) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Zoom
* Pros:
	+ User-friendly interface
	+ Comprehensive set of features
	+ Scalable for large deployments
	+ Integrates with many third-party tools
	+ Reliable and stable
* Cons:
	+ Proprietary and closed-source
	+ Limited control over data
	+ Can be expensive for large teams
	+ Limited customization options
### Jitsi Meet
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Self-hosting option for full data control
	+ Highly customizable
	+ Integrates with many open-source tools
	+ Community-driven development
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve for setup and configuration
	+ Limited features compared to Zoom
	+ May require more technical expertise for maintenance
	+ Not as polished or user-friendly as Zoom
	+ Limited support for certain browsers or devices

## When to Choose Each
Zoom is suitable for teams that prioritize ease of use, a comprehensive set of features, and scalability. It's ideal for large teams or enterprises that need a reliable and stable video conferencing solution. On the other hand, Jitsi Meet is perfect for teams that value data ownership, customization, and cost-effectiveness. It's suitable for small to medium-sized teams, open-source enthusiasts, or organizations with specific security and compliance requirements.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Zoom meeting data in CSV format using the Zoom API or web interface.
2. Set up a Jitsi Meet server, either self-hosted or through a cloud provider.
3. Use the Jitsi Meet API or import tools to migrate your meeting data from Zoom.
4. Configure Jitsi Meet to match your team's requirements, including authentication, authorization, and feature settings.
5. Test your Jitsi Meet setup to ensure a smooth transition for your team.

## Our Take
Jitsi Meet is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Jitsi Meet's scalability can be affected by the quality of the server and network infrastructure. However, for teams that value data ownership and customization, Jitsi Meet is a viable alternative to Zoom, and we recommend switching if you have a small to medium-sized team, prioritize self-hosting, and don't need Zoom's comprehensive set of features.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced features like virtual whiteboards or polls.
* Open-source enthusiasts who value customization and community-driven development.
* Organizations with specific security and compliance requirements that necessitate self-hosting.
* Teams with limited budgets that want a free and open-source video conferencing solution.
* Developers who need a highly customizable video conferencing platform for integration with other tools.

## FAQ
### Can I use Jitsi Meet for large-scale deployments?
Jitsi Meet can handle large meetings, but it may require more configuration and optimization to ensure scalability.
### Is Jitsi Meet compatible with all browsers and devices?
Jitsi Meet has limited support for certain browsers or devices, so it's essential to test compatibility before switching.
### Can I integrate Jitsi Meet with third-party tools?
Jitsi Meet integrates with many open-source tools, but support for proprietary tools may be limited.
### Is Jitsi Meet secure and compliant with regulations?
Jitsi Meet provides robust security features, including end-to-end encryption, and can be configured to meet specific compliance requirements.
### Can I customize Jitsi Meet to match my team's branding?
Jitsi Meet offers high customization options, including branding, to match your team's requirements.

	+ Large user community
	+ Regular updates with new features
* Cons:

## When to Choose Each

On the other hand, Mattermost is perfect for teams that value data ownership, customization, and self-hosting. It's suitable for large teams, development teams, or organizations with specific security and compliance requirements.

## Migration Path

2. Set up a Mattermost server and configure the necessary integrations and plugins.
3. Use the Mattermost Import tool to import your exported Microsoft Teams data.
4. Configure user accounts, channels, and permissions in Mattermost.
5. Test and verify that all data has been successfully migrated.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a reliable and feature-rich collaboration experience. However, it's essential to note that Mattermost's self-hosting option requires technical expertise, which can be a barrier for some teams. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's mobile app functionality can be limited compared to Microsoft Teams.

Mattermost's architecture is designed to be highly scalable and customizable, making it an excellent choice for large teams and organizations with specific requirements. However, this customization can come at the cost of complexity, and teams should carefully evaluate their needs before switching.

For teams prioritizing data ownership, customization, and self-hosting, Mattermost is an excellent choice. However, teams deeply integrated with Microsoft Office tools and requiring a user-friendly interface may find Microsoft Teams more suitable. We recommend switching to Mattermost if you value data ownership and customization, but if you're heavily invested in the Microsoft ecosystem, it might be more convenient to stick with Microsoft Teams.

## Who Should Switch

title: Google Workspace vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Google Workspace vs Nextcloud

## Overview

Google suite of cloud productivity tools including Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Meet, and Calendar. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Nextcloud is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Google Workspace costs $6-$18/user/month; Nextcloud is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Google Workspace is Proprietary; Nextcloud is AGPL 3.0
- **Data ownership**: Nextcloud can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Nextcloud eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Nextcloud has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Google Workspace | Nextcloud |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $6-$18/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$300/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,200/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Google Workspace

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Nextcloud

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [nextcloud/server](https://github.com/nextcloud/server) * ~27k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Google Workspace if:** Google Workspace is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Nextcloud if:** Nextcloud is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Google Workspace in its standard export format, review Nextcloud import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Nextcloud is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Google Workspace tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Nextcloud instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Google Workspace, switching to self-hosted Nextcloud will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Google Workspace until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Google Workspace paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Nextcloud free to use?
Yes. Nextcloud is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Google Workspace to Nextcloud?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Google Workspace data, follow the Nextcloud import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Nextcloud get regular updates?
Yes. Nextcloud has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Nextcloud without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Nextcloud development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Google Workspace](https://workspace.google.com) and [Nextcloud](https://nextcloud.com) before making decisions.*
